name: Correct bills and resolve billing disputes
summary: After an invoice goes out, some charges have to change. Terminals reweigh or inspect freight and find it heavier or in a higher class than the bill said, refused or redelivered freight earns extra charges, and customers dispute rates, reweighs and accessorials. Billing auditors check the evidence, get rate answers from the pricing desk and proof from terminals, and issue rebills or credit notes that supervisors approve above a limit. Disputes wait days for pricing and for customers, and the invoice stays unpaid until they are settled.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with a central billing centre whose auditors handle rebills, credit notes and billing disputes.
baseline.notes: The workflow starts when a correction request reaches the billing auditors' queue and ends when a corrected invoice is posted or the charge is upheld. Collection of the corrected invoice is in collections.

trigger: A weight and inspection certificate, a refused-freight or redelivery charge, or a billing dispute from a customer or from collections reaches the corrections queue.
end_state: A rebill or credit note is posted and sent, the charge is upheld and accepted, or the request is closed with no change.

volume.seasonality: Higher in January to March when general rate increases and contract renewals take effect, and after the autumn peak.

evidence.note: Organisation file's volume, about 6% of LTL bills; vendor sources claim far higher discrepancy rates on shippers' side, so this is a lower, carrier-side count of cases opened. Author's estimate.

surge.cause: Annual general rate increase and contract renewal season

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file's process entry; the author considers a tripling high but found no evidence to change it.

Reweigh and inspection processing is a documented billing task. FTE: all 10 billing auditors in the organisation file, against about 22 implied by hands-on time of about 19 minutes per case; see assumptions.
Credit approvals and the weekly error report; author's estimate.
About 1,000 pricing disputes a month at about 19 minutes each; not listed in the organisation file's process entry.
Proof for accessorial disputes and refused freight; not listed in the organisation file's process entry.
Escalated disputes, about 200 a month at 30 to 60 minutes; not listed in the organisation file's process entry.
Large credits and write-offs; not listed in the organisation file's process entry.

systems.name: Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Document imaging for bills of lading and delivery receipts
ERP general ledger, payables and receivables
EDI gateway (204 tenders, 211 bills of lading, 214 status, 210 invoices)
Email, phone system and contact centre software

steps.name: Open and classify the correction request
steps.description: A billing auditor opens the next item in the corrections queue: a weight and inspection certificate from a terminal, a refused-freight or redelivery charge, a customer's dispute email or portal message, or a dispute passed on by collections. The auditor links it to the PRO number and sorts it by type.
inputs: reweigh certificate, accessorial notice or dispute

error.defect_description: Request linked to the wrong PRO or invoice.

evidence.note: Shares follow the organisation file's triggers; author's estimate.

steps.name: Compare the inspection certificate with the original bill
steps.description: The auditor compares the weight, dimensions and class on the terminal's weight and inspection certificate with the original bill and the shipper's figures, checks that the change is outside the tolerance and that the scale or dimensioner record is attached.

error.defect_description: Correction accepted without a valid scale ticket, which the customer later disputes.

evidence.note: Rate clerks process reweighs and inspections from terminals; a Canadian LTL carrier reweighs when the weight differs significantly and corrects charges to the actual weight. Shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Re-rate the bill with the corrected weight or class
steps.description: The rating engine re-prices the bill with the corrected weight, dimensions or class under the customer's agreement and shows the difference from the original charge.

evidence.note: Common practice; author's estimate.

steps.name: Verify an added accessorial charge
steps.description: For a refused, redelivered or stored shipment, the auditor checks the terminal's notes, delivery attempt scans and the rules tariff item to confirm that the charge applies and that the right party will be billed.

error.defect_description: Charge billed to the consignee instead of the shipper.

evidence.note: Vendor blog: unexpected accessorials such as redelivery and inside delivery are a main source of invoice discrepancies; shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Pull the invoice and its documents
steps.description: The auditor gathers the invoice, the signed bill of lading and delivery receipt images, any inspection certificate, the pricing agreement or quote and the customer's own calculation, and records the disputed amount on the dispute log so collections holds the invoice.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide the cause of the dispute
steps.description: The auditor compares the customer's claim with the documents and decides which kind of problem it is: a pricing or discount error, a contested reweigh or reclassification, a contested accessorial, a bill sent to the wrong party or terms, or a charge that is correct.

error.defect_description: Cause misjudged; the case loops back after the customer objects.

evidence.note: Vendor claim that about half of LTL discrepancies come from location-related accessorials and half from reweigh and reclassification; this carrier's mix, with a pricing share, is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send the pricing discrepancy to the pricing desk
steps.description: The auditor sends the pricing analyst the PRO numbers, the agreement item the customer quotes and the rate the engine applied, and asks which price is right.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm the correct rate and fix the agreement
steps.description: The pricing analyst checks the signed agreement, quote and renewal history, confirms with the account executive what was promised, corrects the agreement in the rating engine and lists any other bills affected by the same error.

error.defect_description: Agreement corrected for the disputed lane only, leaving similar lanes wrong.

evidence.note: Pricing analysts give billing queries lower priority than quotes and renewals; author's estimate.

steps.name: Weigh the reweigh evidence against the customer's
steps.description: The auditor compares the carrier's scale ticket, dimensioner record and inspection photos with the customer's packing list, product specifications or own scale record, and decides whether to keep or reverse the correction.

error.defect_description: Correction kept although the scale record is incomplete.

evidence.note: Reweighs and reclassifications are a frequent source of re-rates; decision split is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Request proof of the accessorial from the terminal
steps.description: The auditor asks the terminal that performed the service for proof: the driver's notes, handheld arrival and departure times, appointment records or photos of a residential or limited-access delivery.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm the event from terminal records
steps.description: The terminal service clerk looks up the delivery attempt, the driver's handheld times and notes, and asks the driver or dock supervisor if records are thin, then replies with what happened and any photos or signed documents.

evidence.note: Terminal clerks answer billing queries between customer calls; author's estimate.

steps.name: Draft a response upholding the charge
steps.description: The auditor writes to the customer explaining why the charge stands, attaching the scale ticket, inspection photos, delivery notes or agreement item, and tells collections the dispute is answered.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Customer reviews the response
steps.description: The customer's accounts payable team or freight audit provider reviews the explanation and either pays the invoice or comes back with more evidence or a request for a goodwill credit.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Account executive decides on an escalated dispute
steps.description: The account executive reviews the disputed charge, the account's revenue and the relationship, talks to the customer and decides whether to keep the charge or give a goodwill credit, often agreeing a fix to the customer's agreement for future shipments.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; account executives travel and handle disputes between sales calls.

steps.name: Prepare the rebill or credit note
steps.description: The auditor enters the correction in the TMS: a rebill at the corrected charge, a credit note for the difference, or a cancel-and-rebill to the right bill-to party, with a reason code that feeds the error report.

error.defect_description: Wrong amount or reason code entered.

evidence.note: Approval limits and shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Approve a credit above the auditor's limit
steps.description: The billing supervisor reviews the credit note with its reason and documents and approves it in the TMS or sends it back for correction. Approval keeps the person who agrees a credit separate from the person who enters it.

control.basis: Credit note approval limits in the finance delegation of authority

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Credit manager approves a large credit or write-off
steps.description: For a large credit or a write-off of a disputed balance, the credit and collections manager reviews the account's history and the dispute file and approves or refuses it.

control.basis: Finance delegation of authority for credits and write-offs

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Post the correction and issue the corrected invoice
steps.description: The nightly run posts the rebill or credit note to accounts receivable and revenue and sends the corrected invoice by the customer's usual channel.

evidence.note: Common practice; author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the case with the customer and collections
steps.description: The auditor tells the customer and the collections clerk that the correction is issued, asks collections to release the dispute hold on the invoice and closes the case on the dispute log.

next.condition: pricing or entry error to report

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Log the root cause on the weekly error report
steps.description: The billing supervisor adds pricing and bill entry errors to the weekly error report sent to the pricing manager and billing team leads, so that agreements are fixed and clerks are coached.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Reweigh within tolerance
exceptions.description: The inspection certificate shows a change too small or unsupported, so no rebill is issued.

exceptions.name: Pricing error dispute
exceptions.description: The customer quotes an agreement item the engine did not apply; the case waits two to seven days for the pricing desk.

exceptions.name: Contested reweigh
exceptions.description: The customer sends product specifications or its own scale record; the auditor reverses or upholds the correction.

exceptions.name: Escalated to the account executive
exceptions.description: The customer rejects the explanation and the account executive decides on a goodwill credit.

exceptions.name: Large credit or write-off
exceptions.description: The credit is above the supervisor's limit and goes to the credit and collections manager.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from request in the corrections queue to correction posted or charge upheld

evidence.note: Reweigh corrections clear in one to three days and disputes in one to three weeks; author's estimate.
Shipper-side and vendor sources report 25 to 40% of LTL invoices with re-rates or discrepancies for some shippers; the carrier-wide share of cases opened is the author's estimate and much lower.

pain_points.description: Reweighs and reclassifications are the largest single cause of corrections and of disputes, and each contested one needs evidence from the terminal scale or dimensioner.

evidence.note: Shippers report up to one in four shipments reweighed or reclassified; vendor claim that about half of discrepancies are reweigh and reclassification.

pain_points.description: Pricing disputes wait days for the pricing desk, while the invoice sits unpaid and on dispute hold in collections.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common carrier practice.

pain_points.description: Small accessorial disputes cost more to investigate than the charge is worth.

evidence.note: Vendor blog: auditors may spend an hour on a $10 issue.

assumptions: The mix of request types follows the organisation file's triggers: 35% reweigh and inspection corrections, 8% refused-freight charges, 37% customer disputes and 20% disputes passed on by collections.
Accessorials found at delivery (liftgate, appointment, waiting time) are added before invoicing in the rating process; the organisation file has no link from delivery execution to this process.
Pricing analysts, terminal service clerks, account executives and the credit manager take part although the organisation file's process entry lists only billing auditors and the billing supervisor.

Hands-on time is about 19 auditor minutes per case (about 6 for a reweigh correction, about 30 for a dispute), which implies about 22 billing auditor FTE at 9,000 cases a month against 10 in the organisation file. Either the auditor headcount is too low or the case count is closer to 4,000 a month; in practice customer service and collections clerks also do part of the dispute research. The gap is left visible rather than hidden by shortening step times.
The pricing error report is produced only for the about 10% of corrected cases with a pricing or entry error, although the interface lists it under every corrected outcome.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file.

sources.title: Night Rate Clerk (Roadrunner Freight, Milwaukee) job posting
sources.publisher: Roadrunner Freight, listed on Simplify Jobs
sources.supports: LTL rate clerks use a central auto-rating system to calculate and verify rates on freight bills, hand-rate bills the system cannot rate by applying published pricing agreements and calculating accessorials, process reweighs and inspections from terminals, talk to terminal staff about problem freight bills, help billing staff classify commodities under the NMFC, and finish rating before a daily revenue cut-off of about 5 a.m.; requires experience with bills of lading, freight bills and tariffs and 40 words-per-minute typing and ten-key skills.

sources.title: Tariff Update: Reweigh Administrative Fee & QC Fuel Surcharge
sources.supports: A Canadian LTL carrier reweighs shipments when there is a significant weight difference and corrects the freight charges to the actual weight; from October 2025 it adds a $20 administrative fee when the reweigh is 35 lb or more above the documented weight.

sources.title: How Accurate Shipping Data Is Transforming LTL Outcomes
sources.supports: Shippers report that up to one in four LTL shipments came back reweighed or reclassified before they measured freight themselves (one fell to 1% re-rates after using a dimensioner); NMFTA estimates 70 to 80% of LTL freight is classified by density alone; measurements should flow into the bill of lading digitally rather than on paper. Sponsored article promoting one carrier.

sources.title: Common LTL Invoicing Challenges and How to Address Them
sources.supports: Vendor claim, from industry veterans, that 30 to 40% of LTL invoices contain discrepancies, about half from location-related accessorial fees (residential, limited access) and half from reweigh and reclassification; manual data entry leads to inaccuracies, delays and disputes, and auditors may spend an hour on a $10 issue. Year of publication not shown on the page; 2024 is the author's estimate.
